children.text: The seat of the Archdiocese of Cebu, whose façade and
bell tower survived the
bombing before the church was rebuilt after the war. Pair it with the cathedral museum across the plaza to take in more than 400 years of Catholic history in Cebu at an unhurried pace.
Cebu Metropolitan Cathedral is the mother church of Cebu, home to the cathedra, the seat of the archbishop who leads the Archdiocese of Cebu. It stands on P. Burgos Street in the old downtown, about
northeast of the Basilica del Santo Niño and Magellan's Cross, a walk of just over
5 minutes

. Its official name is the Metropolitan Cathedral and Parish of Saint Vitalis of Milan, and it is dedicated to the Most Holy Name of Jesus and to St. Vitalis. If the Basilica del Santo Niño, home of the Holy Child image, is the pilgrimage shrine, this is the mother church where the archdiocese holds its major liturgies, and many travelers mix the two up.
Its history goes back to the earliest days of Spanish settlement. Tradition holds that it began when Legazpi's expedition built a church of St. Vitalis near the fort in
, and according to the National Historical Commission marker, the first cathedral, built of wood and nipa palm, became the center of the Diocese of Cebu in
. Work on a stone church began in the late 17th century, but it stalled several times as bishops died and money ran short, stopped again with the revolution of
, and the church was finally consecrated only in
. When Cebu was raised to an archdiocese in
, it became the metropolitan cathedral it is named today.
Its greatest ordeal was World War II. Allied bombing of Cebu in
destroyed most of the church, leaving only the façade, the bell tower and the surrounding walls. Reconstruction began in
under Archbishop Julio Rosales, and the church took its present form around
to a design by architect José Ma. Zaragoza. That is why the weather-darkened façade and the bell tower built in
date from the Spanish era, while the nave inside is a postwar space. The National Historical Commission installed a historical marker in
, and a National Museum Important Cultural Property marker followed in
March 2023

Unlike the ever-crowded Basilica del Santo Niño, the cathedral is fairly quiet on weekdays, making it a good fit for travelers who want to take their time with Spanish-era church architecture and Cebu's church history. The cathedral alone takes
30 minutes to 1 hour
, adding the cathedral museum across the plaza brings it to
2–3 hours

, and combined with the Basilica del Santo Niño, Magellan's Cross and Fort San Pedro it makes a half-day walking tour of the old town. Entry is free, and anyone is welcome, Catholic or not, as long as they are respectful.

The three-lobed pediment at the top of the façade is carved with floral reliefs, the IHS monogram for the name of Jesus and a pair of griffins, and the Spanish royal coat of arms is set in low relief above the main door. The low, thick walls, built to withstand typhoons, stayed standing through the
bombing. Stand at an angle from the left corner of the plaza to fit the façade and the bell tower into one frame.

blocks.title: Bell tower that survived the war

children.text: The octagonal bell tower to the left of the façade was built in

and, together with the façade, is a Spanish-era survivor of the war. Look up to see its red dome, clock and the bells inside its arched openings; after sunset the lights give it a different face from the daytime. Walk around toward the side entrance by the tower to see the octagonal body up close.

Step inside and, at the end of a bright nave lined with balconies on both sides and chandeliers, you will see a golden altarpiece (retablo) with Christ on the cross beneath a sunburst IHS emblem. Refurbished after the war, the space is bright and open, unlike the dim interiors of older Baroque churches. When no Mass is on, sit quietly in a rear pew and take it all in.
A wall of the cathedral holds a stained-glass window of St. Pedro Calungsod, a young catechist from the Visayas who was canonized in
. He is the second Filipino saint after Lorenzo Ruiz and is especially dear to the people of Cebu. His name is written beneath the window, so it is easy to find.

On one side of the grounds is an adoration chapel whose entrance is decorated with modern stained glass, where the faithful stay and pray in silence. In front of the Our Lady of Lourdes grotto in the courtyard you can see people lighting candles and praying. Please refrain from talking and taking photos inside the adoration chapel.

The two-story building across the plaza is a bahay na bato (a house with a coral-stone ground floor and a wooden upper floor) that served as the cathedral rectory in the 19th century, and it opened as the Cathedral Museum of Cebu, the archdiocesan museum, around

. Inside are a relic chapel holding about 70 first-class relics, six galleries upstairs, a silver-clad tabernacle and altar, old vestments and chalices, a re-created priest's bedroom, Spanish-era church building materials and old bells in the back garden.

blocks.title: Cardinal Vidal and the historical marker

children.text: Cardinal Ricardo Vidal, who led the Archdiocese of Cebu from

, is laid to rest in the cathedral mausoleum, and the museum has a gallery of his personal effects. The National Historical Commission marker on the front wall sums up the cathedral's history in Filipino, and it is fun to match the dates you have read here against it on the spot.

Cebu is hot and humid all year, with normal temperatures generally around
. The drier season from
December to May
is best for walking, and
December–February
is relatively cool. From
March to May

the midday heat is intense, so visit the cathedral and museum early in the morning or late in the afternoon. The church interior and the museum are indoors, which also makes them a good rainy-day plan.
The mood also changes with the church calendar. During Sinulog (Fiesta Señor) on the third Sunday of
January
(around
January 17, 2027

), the whole old town fills with crowds centered on the neighboring Basilica del Santo Niño, and roads are closed. During Holy Week the cathedral hosts the Chrism Mass that gathers the archdiocese's priests, and on the night of Holy Thursday it fills with pilgrims doing Visita Iglesia, visiting church after church. From
December 16 to 24
, Simbang Gabi, the dawn Masses leading up to Christmas, are held.
June–November
is the rainy and typhoon season. Typhoons have caused major damage in Cebu, as Typhoon Tino did in
November 2025
, so be prepared for canceled flights and ferries and flooded roads. Since the northern Cebu earthquake of
September 30, 2025
, some heritage sites in the old town may be under repair.

The area around the cathedral is downtown along Colon Street, with plenty of budget and mid-range hotels and hostels that make it easy to explore the old town on foot, at about
per night. For polished chain hotels, the areas around IT Park or Ayala Center Cebu are better, but the cathedral is
20–40 minutes
away by car. If you are combining the trip with a beach stay, you can base yourself on Mactan Island and come into the city for a day. Downtown gets quiet at night, so choose a hotel on a main road.

The first dish to name is Cebu lechon (whole roast pig) with its crackling skin. Barbecue served with puso, rice cooked in a pouch of woven young coconut leaves, is also the Cebuano way, and Larsian (Sugbo Sentro) near Fuente Osmeña is a long-standing barbecue alley lined with grilled-skewer stalls. The old town has plenty of cheap local eateries (carinderias), but on a first visit, start with clean places that are busy with customers. Popular souvenirs are dried mangoes and the Cebuano pastry otap.
Enter "Cebu Metropolitan Cathedral" exactly in your map app. Searching for "Santo Niño" will lead you to the basilica about
away.
Weekday mornings are the quietest. On Sundays and on days with archdiocesan events, Masses follow one after another and it is hard to look around the nave.
Mass schedules may change from week to week, so check the cathedral's Facebook page (katedralsasugbo) or the parish office's announcements.
The museum is open roughly
, but opening times and closing days differ between sources, so confirm on site and bring cash for admission.
Wear clothes that cover your shoulders and knees. You may be turned away in a sleeveless top or short shorts.
During Mass, avoid flash photography and loud talk, and do not take close-up photos of people praying.
To fit the façade and bell tower into one frame, shoot at an angle from the left corner of the plaza, and aim for the moment the lights come on just after sunset.
Combine the cathedral with the Basilica del Santo Niño, Magellan's Cross and Fort San Pedro on a morning walk to beat the heat. Bring water and a parasol.
Carry plenty of small bills and coins for donations, candles and jeepney fares.
On
September 30, 2025

, the very night after a new archbishop's installation Mass was held here that morning, a magnitude 6.9 earthquake struck off the coast of northern Cebu. The badly damaged churches are concentrated in northern Cebu, and the cathedral has continued to hold Masses and archdiocesan events since then, but the archdiocese ordered safety inspections of all churches, and some heritage sites, such as the Magellan's Cross pavilion next door, have restricted access. Check the latest notices before you visit.
Pickpocketing and snatch theft are common around the plaza and Colon Street. Don't walk with your phone in your hand, and wear your bag in front.
Vendors selling candles, flowers or rosaries may follow you. Politely decline if you don't need anything, and ask the price first if you do want to buy.
Downtown empties out after dark. Avoid walking late at night and use Grab instead.
Make sure taxi drivers turn on the meter, and at the airport take a Grab or an official airport taxi.
In the rainy season heavy downpours flood the roads, and in the dry season the midday heat is intense. Check the weather forecast and carry water.
This is a place of worship. Don't sit on the altar steps or take photos while blocking people who are praying.
